title: Forty Days: A Bible Study for Lent
subtitle: A five-session study from Ash Wednesday to Holy Saturday on dust, the wilderness, returning to God, the way of the cross, and the darkest week.
summary:
Lent is the forty days before Easter, kept by many churches and not by others. This study is for a church or small group walking from Ash Wednesday to Easter, and for anyone who has never kept Lent and wonders why anyone would. Its first session begins where Ash Wednesday begins, with the sentence spoken to the first man, "For dust you are, and to dust you shall return" (Genesis 3:19), and with the psalm that says the LORD "is mindful that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14). The second follows Jesus into the wilderness, where he answered hunger and temptation with the words Moses spoke about the manna. The third hears Joel's call to return and prays Psalm 51 as David's confession, refusing the idea that repentance means punishing yourself. The fourth reads the call to take up the cross in Mark 8, beside Isaiah's suffering servant. The fifth walks through Mark 14 and 15 and ends where the women ended, at a sealed tomb on the Sabbath, with Easter morning still ahead. Each session is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation beyond reading the leader's primer once.

The study doesn't settle whether Christians should keep Lent. Some churches receive the season as a gift from the early church; others hold that believers are free of any season Scripture doesn't command, and they have watched the custom harden into a law or turn into a show. Both are stated in their strongest form. Fasting comes with the health cautions first, and no one needs to fast from food to keep this study. Nor does the study stand outside its subject: the church has turned Lent into a diet with a religious label, a contest over who gave up the most, and a season of guilt, and it has also let fasting itself slip away and forgotten what it was for. No one leads this study from above either failure.
audience: Churches and small groups keeping Lent, and anyone who has never kept it and wonders why anyone would

sessions.title: Dust
sessions.aim: To begin Lent where Ash Wednesday begins, with the plain truth that we will die, and to find in Genesis 3 and Psalm 103 that the God who names us dust is also the Father who remembers it, so that the room can look at death without denial and without despair.
sessions.summary:
On Ash Wednesday, in many churches, a minister marks each forehead with ash and speaks words drawn from Genesis 3:19 over every person in the line, child and grandparent alike. Most of us arrange our days so that we rarely think about dying, and not all of that is cowardice. But many churches have long begun Lent by saying aloud the sentence we spend our lives avoiding.

The sentence comes from a hard chapter. After the man and woman have eaten what God told them not to eat, God says to the man, "For dust you are, and to dust you shall return" (Genesis 3:19). Death enters the story as the consequence of turning from the source of life. Yet before the man and woman leave the garden, God clothes them (Genesis 3:21), and Psalm 103, which bears David's name, turns the dust into a reason for mercy: "For He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14). Our days are like grass, and the loving devotion of the LORD runs from everlasting to everlasting. Lent begins with dust because Easter is God's answer to death itself, and a church that won't say the word death on Wednesday will have little to say on Sunday.

keyScripture.why: God tells the man after the fall that he will toil "until you return to the ground" (Genesis 3:19), and the verse ends with the words many churches speak on Ash Wednesday: "For dust you are, and to dust you shall return." Two verses later God clothes the man and woman (Genesis 3:21). The dust is the truth about us, but it is not the whole truth about God.

discussion.q: When did you first understand that you would die someday, and how did the adults around you talk about death, or avoid talking about it?
discussion.behind: Begin with what people inherited: some grew up where death was spoken of plainly and some where it was never mentioned. Don't correct anything yet. Someone in the room may have buried a person they love this year, so never call on anyone, and let anyone pass. Go first, briefly.

discussion.q: Read Genesis 2:7 and Genesis 3:17-21 aloud. What does the dust mean in the first passage, what does it mean in the second, and what does God do in Genesis 3:21 before the man and woman leave the garden?
discussion.behind: The dust is first the material God shaped and breathed into, and only later the place we return to. Death enters as the consequence of turning from the source of life, and the chapter doesn't soften it. Then God clothes them: mercy at work inside the judgment, a pattern that runs through the whole of Lent.

discussion.q: Psalm 103 says the LORD "is mindful that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14). Why would our frailty be a reason for God's compassion rather than his contempt? What would change if you believed that about yourself?
discussion.behind: Many people assume God is disappointed in their weakness. The psalm says the opposite, in a father's terms: "As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him" (Psalm 103:13). For anyone whose own father was not compassionate, let the psalm define the word rather than the memory.

discussion.q: Where do you see our culture, our churches, and your own calendar working to avoid the fact of death? What does the avoidance cost?
discussion.behind: Keep this from becoming a complaint about other people. Ernest Becker argued in The Denial of Death that much human striving is a flight from mortality, and the room will recognize the pattern in reputations, achievements, and full calendars. Then bring it home: funerals hurried toward celebration, Christians who can talk about heaven but not about dying. Name your own avoidance first.

discussion.q: The letter to the Hebrews says Christ shared our flesh and blood to "free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death" (Hebrews 2:15). What would it look like to live this Lent a little less afraid?
discussion.behind: Don't promise anyone fearlessness, and don't treat the fear of death as a lack of faith; Scripture calls death an enemy. The freedom Hebrews describes rests on a person who went through death ahead of us, not on pretending. Anyone whose anxiety needs more than a study deserves real help without shame. Close by reading Psalm 103:17 aloud.

objections.objection: Religion is a way of coping with death, and Ash Wednesday proves it. You remind people they're going to die and then sell them heaven.
objections.response: Much of this is true, and it should be said first. Ernest Becker argued that a great deal of human culture is built to keep the terror of death out of sight, and some religion does work that way, offering a mood instead of a hope. But Ash Wednesday doesn't soothe. It puts dust on your forehead and says the plain sentence aloud. The Bible Christians read includes Ecclesiastes, where "all come from dust, and all return to dust" (Ecclesiastes 3:20), and it refuses to call death a friend: "The last enemy to be destroyed is death" (1 Corinthians 15:26). Christian hope is a claim about something that happened to a dead man's body, and a claim like that can be weighed. The study of the resurrection, /studyguides/resurrection, weighs it with the skeptic in mind.

objections.objection: Jesus told us not to make our devotion visible, and many churches read that very passage on Ash Wednesday. Walking around with ash on your forehead is exactly what he warned against.
objections.response: The warning is real and specific. Jesus said of the hypocrites that "they disfigure their faces to show men they are fasting" (Matthew 6:16), and some faithful Christians decline the ashes for exactly this reason. Those who receive them answer that the ash is a shared confession rather than a display: the minister says the same words to everyone in the line, and everyone in the line is mortal and needs mercy. Both sides are trying to obey the same chapter, and this study doesn't settle the question. If your church imposes ashes, receive them or decline them in freedom; if it doesn't, read Genesis 3:19 and Psalm 103 at home that day. "Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind" (Romans 14:5).

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What would you live differently this week if you believed both that you are dust and that God remembers it?
sessions.practice: This week, read Psalm 103:13-17 aloud each morning. Each evening, pray Psalm 90:12, "So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom," and write one honest line about where the day went. Choose one thing to set down for Lent and one thing to take up. If you plan to fast from food, start with your health: talk with a doctor first if you've had an eating disorder or a long struggle with food, if you have diabetes or another medical condition or take regular medication, if you're pregnant or nursing or under eighteen, or if fasting has become about weight or control. You can fast from something else instead, and no one is less faithful for it; /help/fasting says more, and none of this is medical advice. If Ash Wednesday is still ahead, go to your church's service if it holds one, or read Joel 2:12-17 and Psalm 51 that day. The printable Forty Days With Mark plan, /plans#lent-with-mark, begins on Ash Wednesday. If this week's reading stirs thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988, or 911 in an emergency, and tell someone you trust.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord God, you formed us from the dust of the ground and breathed your life into us, and you have not forgotten what we are made of. We confess that we have lived as if we would never die, and spent our days on what cannot last. Teach us to number our days. Be the compassion of a father to those here who are grieving and to those waiting on news they are afraid to hear. Your Son shared our flesh and went down into death so that we would not be slaves to the fear of it. Hold us this Lent between the dust and the morning. Amen.
reflection: What did I learn about death growing up, and how has it shaped the way I live now?
Do I believe God looks at my frailty with compassion or with disappointment, and what in Psalm 103 speaks to that?
What am I spending my days on that I wouldn't choose if I numbered them?
sessions.teaching:
Ash Wednesday is a strange way to begin anything. In many churches a minister marks each forehead with ash, often in the sign of a cross, and speaks words drawn from Genesis 3:19 over every person in the line, the child and the grandparent, the healthy and the dying. The ash is customarily made by burning the palm branches from the year before, and in some churches the minister says instead Jesus' first words of preaching in Mark's Gospel, his call to repent and believe the gospel (Mark 1:15). Either way, the season begins with a sentence most of us spend our lives arranging not to hear.

Be fair to the arranging, because not all of it is cowardice. There is work to do and there are children to raise, a mind that dwells on death all day is stuck rather than wise, and some in this room already live beside death and need no reminder. What Ash Wednesday asks is smaller and harder than gloom: that we stop pretending.

The sentence comes from a hard chapter. The man and woman have eaten from the tree God told them not to eat from, and God speaks to the man of toil and thorns and sweat, "until you return to the ground" (Genesis 3:19), and then the words themselves: "For dust you are, and to dust you shall return." To hear them rightly, go back a chapter: "Then the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being" (Genesis 2:7). Dust is what God chose to shape, and it lives because he breathed into it. Death enters when the creature turns from the one whose breath keeps it alive, and Genesis doesn't soften that. Yet before the man and woman leave the garden, "the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them" (Genesis 3:21). Mercy is already at work inside the judgment.

Psalm 103, which bears David's name, holds the two truths in a single breath: "As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him. For He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust" (Psalm 103:13-14). Here the dust is the reason for God's gentleness, though many of us have spent years assuming it was the reason for his disappointment. Then the psalm looks straight at mortality, "As for man, his days are like grass" (Psalm 103:15), and turns: "But from everlasting to everlasting the loving devotion of the LORD extends to those who fear Him" (Psalm 103:17). Our days are short, and his love is not.

We need both halves, and most of us are fluent in neither. In 1973 the anthropologist Ernest Becker published The Denial of Death, arguing that much human striving is a flight from the knowledge that we will die, organized into projects meant to make us feel we will last: the reputation, the fortune, the work with our name on it. He saw the symptom truly. The letter to the Hebrews had named it long before, speaking of people "who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death" (Hebrews 2:15), and it answers with a person, which Becker did not: Christ shared our flesh and blood "so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death" (Hebrews 2:14).

Before we point at the culture, we should look at ourselves. We hurry funerals toward celebration, we speak of heaven in a way that skips the grave, and we fill our calendars as busily as anyone. Pastors can be the worst at it, because they handle death for a living and can go years without letting it touch them. Ash Wednesday puts the same dust on the pastor's forehead as on everyone else's, and that is part of its mercy.

So why begin Lent with dust? Because Easter isn't God's answer to sadness. It is his answer to death. Paul wrote, "The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven" (1 Corinthians 15:47), and promised that "just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man" (1 Corinthians 15:49). A church that rushes past the dust will find the empty tomb strangely weightless, a happy ending to a story whose stakes were never told.

For some in this room the words will land differently. If you are grieving, Ash Wednesday tells you nothing you didn't know, but it offers company: a whole church saying aloud what you have been carrying alone. If you have never thought much about dying, the prayer that bears Moses' name is worth praying for forty days: "So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom" (Psalm 90:12). And if you have been in a place dark enough that you've thought about not wanting to live, the dust is not the last word spoken over you; before the psalm says we are dust, it says the LORD has a father's compassion (Psalm 103:13). Please tell someone tonight, and know that you can call or text 988 at any hour. No one here is asked to feel anything on cue. You are asked to believe two things at once: you are dust, and you are remembered.

scriptureStudy.note: "For dust you are, and to dust you shall return" (Genesis 3:19). The sentence belongs to the judgment after the fall, with its toil and thorns, yet before the chapter ends with the man and woman sent out of the garden, God clothes them (Genesis 3:21).

"For He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14). In this psalm, which bears David's name, our frailty is the reason for God's compassion, and our short days are set against a love that runs "from everlasting to everlasting" (Psalm 103:17).

"You return man to dust, saying, 'Return, O sons of mortals'" (Psalm 90:3). The prayer that bears Moses' name looks at the brevity of life without flinching and asks for one thing: "So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom" (Psalm 90:12).

"All go to one place; all come from dust, and all return to dust" (Ecclesiastes 3:20). The Teacher looks at death as honestly as any skeptic and leaves his own question standing. Scripture makes room for this voice rather than hurrying past it.

Christ "shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death" (Hebrews 2:14). The letter names the fear of death as slavery and answers it with a person who went through death ahead of us.

"What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable" (1 Corinthians 15:42). Paul doesn't deny the dust. He promises that it will be raised: "so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man" (1 Corinthians 15:49).

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the church's long practice of remembering death, which was not meant to make Christians gloomy. Benedict's Rule, written for monks in the sixth century, counts keeping death daily before one's eyes among the tools of the spiritual life. Augustine, in the fourth book of his Confessions, tells of the death of a close friend in his youth and says that he became a great question to himself. Athanasius, in On the Incarnation, argued that because Christ died and rose, death had lost its power, and he pointed to Christians of his day who faced it without the old fear. In the fifteenth century, short books on the art of dying well, the ars moriendi, taught ordinary Christians how to meet death in faith.

Set beside them Ernest Becker's The Denial of Death, which won the Pulitzer Prize in 1974. Becker saw what the monks saw, that the knowledge of death drives much of what we do, but he named no one who could end its slavery. A serious group should ask how the church's remembering of death was meant to make people freer rather than more afraid, and whether it has. Then ask the harder question: where has the church taught you to hurry past the grave, and what did you lose?
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose that on the first night, after Genesis 3:19 is read, a woman whose husband died in the autumn says quietly that she doesn't need ashes to remember she is dust; she has lived with it every day since the funeral. A few minutes later a young man who came because a friend invited him admits that he has never thought much about dying and isn't sure he wants to start.

You will want to comfort her quickly and to persuade him. Do neither. Thank them both, because each has said something true, and read Psalm 103:13-17 aloud, slowly. For her, the psalm adds company and a God who is mindful of the dust she has been living with; for him, Psalm 90:12 frames numbering our days as wisdom rather than gloom. Afterward, speak with her privately, ask how she is doing, and mention the care page /help/grief and the grief study, /studyguides/grief.

Use this to show the room that the same words land differently in different lives, and that the church's task is to say them truthfully to everyone at once.

sessions.title: The Wilderness
sessions.aim: To read Jesus' forty days in the wilderness beside Israel's forty years, so that the room sees hunger and temptation as places where God teaches his people to live by his word, and to practice a small fast, safely and quietly, as hunger turned toward God.
sessions.summary:
Jesus is baptized, the heavens open, and a voice says, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!" (Matthew 3:17). Matthew's next sentence is, "Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil" (Matthew 4:1). The beloved Son goes hungry for forty days, and the tempter comes with three offers, each a shortcut to something good: bread on his own terms, proof of God's protection, and all the kingdoms of the world for a single act of worship. Jesus answers each from Deuteronomy, where Moses reminded Israel why God had led them through forty years in the wilderness, teaching them with manna "that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD" (Deuteronomy 8:3). Where Israel grumbled, tested God, and bowed to a calf, the Son trusted.

Lent's forty days remember his, though no one should try to repeat what he did. The fast this session asks of anyone is small, one meal or one thing set aside, with the health cautions first, and anyone may fast from something other than food without being less faithful for it. The point is to discover what we have been living on, and to learn a little of what the Son knew in the desert, that the Father's word is enough.

keyScripture.why: "Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. After fasting forty days and forty nights, He was hungry" (Matthew 4:1-2). The beloved Son is led into hunger, and he answers the first temptation with the words Moses spoke about the manna: "Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God" (Matthew 4:4).

discussion.q: What do you reach for first when you're tired, anxious, bored, or lonely? Most of us have a small comfort we turn to without thinking.
discussion.behind: Begin with honesty, not shame. Answers will range from food and the phone to work, shopping, or a drink at the end of the day. For some people food is tender ground because of a long struggle with eating, so never press anyone, and don't joke about dieting. Go first.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 3:16-4:2. What does it tell you that the Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness right after the Father called him beloved?
discussion.behind: Hardship came after the word of love, not instead of it, so a hard season is no proof that God has withdrawn. Mark says the Spirit "drove Jesus into the wilderness" (Mark 1:12). Don't tell anyone that God sent their particular suffering to teach them something; the text is about Jesus and the trust he kept.

discussion.q: Read Deuteronomy 8:2-3. Why would God let his people go hungry, and what did the manna teach them that a full table couldn't?
discussion.behind: The manna came each day, enough for that day (Exodus 16:4), so Israel learned daily dependence. Hunger showed what was in their hearts, and what came out was grumbling (Exodus 16:3). Keep the passage from becoming a theory about anyone's tragedy. It describes a people learning that God's word is as real as bread.

discussion.q: In each temptation the devil offers Jesus something he would receive another way: bread, God's protection, the kingdoms. What makes a shortcut to a good thing a temptation? Where are you offered shortcuts?
discussion.behind: Help the room see the pattern: the good thing on our own terms, now, without trust and without the cross. The devil quotes Scripture in the second temptation (Psalm 91:11-12), bending a psalm of trust into a dare, so knowing verses isn't the same as living by them. Churches know the third offer, the kingdom without the cross, as well as anyone.

discussion.q: If you've chosen a fast for Lent, what has it shown you so far about what you've been living on? If you haven't, is there something you could set aside for a few weeks?
discussion.behind: Keep it voluntary and quiet, as Jesus taught (Matthew 6:16-18). Say plainly that no one is less faithful for fasting from something other than food, repeat the health cautions, and don't count or compare. If anyone mentions fasting to lose weight, gently say that a fast for weight is a diet, however devout it feels, and talk with them privately if you're worried.

objections.objection: Fasting is bad for you, and a God who wants me hungry sounds like a God who wants me miserable.
objections.response: Some of this is true and should be granted first. For some bodies going without food is a real danger, which is why this study puts the health cautions first and counts a fast from something else as a real fast. Christians have sometimes treated the body with contempt, and Scripture itself warns that "harsh treatment of the body" is "of no value against the indulgence of the flesh" (Colossians 2:23). Jesus was mocked as "this glutton and drunkard" (Matthew 11:19) because he ate so freely with sinners. A Christian fast is a short, chosen hunger turned toward God, and it ends in a meal; it earns nothing, and misery is not its point. If your health rules it out, the God who knows your frame isn't disappointed.

objections.objection: Jesus was the Son of God. Of course he resisted temptation. His forty days have nothing to do with my Tuesday afternoon.
objections.response: Start with the difference, because it is real. No one should try to repeat his forty days, and his victory is his, not a technique we can copy. But the letter to the Hebrews insists the temptation was real: "we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin" (Hebrews 4:15). He didn't use his power to feed himself or to force his Father's hand; he answered with words Moses had given the people of God, words open to anyone in this room. And because he stood where we fall, we can "approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need" (Hebrews 4:16). A Tuesday afternoon is exactly that kind of need.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What have you been living on that you would be afraid to go without for a week?
sessions.practice: This week, keep one small fast. If none of the health cautions apply to you, skip one meal, keep drinking water, and spend that time reading Deuteronomy 8:1-10 and praying. Talk with a doctor first if you've had an eating disorder or a long struggle with food, if you have diabetes or another medical condition or take regular medication, if you're pregnant or nursing or under eighteen, or if fasting has become about weight or control; you can fast from something else instead, such as your phone for an evening, and no one is less faithful for it. If you feel faint or unwell, eat; none of this is medical advice. Give what you would have spent to someone who is hungry.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you led your people through the wilderness and fed them with bread they had never known, and you led your beloved Son into the wilderness, and he trusted you there. We confess that we live on many things besides your word, and that we reach for them before we reach for you. Keep us from fasting to be seen, from fasting to bargain, and from fasting in ways that harm the bodies you made. Let our small hunger turn us toward you, and let what we don't eat feed someone who is hungry and didn't choose it. When we are tempted, give us the trust your Son kept. Amen.
reflection: What small comforts do I reach for without thinking, and what do they tell me about what I'm living on?
Where am I tempted to take a shortcut to something good instead of waiting on God?
What would it mean for me this week to live by every word that comes from the mouth of God?
sessions.teaching:
Most temptation arrives quietly, in the afternoon when we're tired or late at night when we're lonely, and it usually offers something good: rest, comfort, relief, control. That's worth noticing before we read the wilderness story, because the temptations Jesus faced were offers to get good things by a different road.

Matthew tells the story in a deliberate order. At Jesus' baptism a voice from heaven says, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!" (Matthew 3:17), and the next sentence is, "Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil" (Matthew 4:1). The wilderness follows the word of love; it is no sign that the Father's love has been withdrawn. Mark says it more starkly: "At once the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness" (Mark 1:12).

The forty days recall Moses on the mountain "forty days and forty nights without eating bread or drinking water" (Exodus 34:28), and Israel's forty years in the desert. Matthew tells the story of Jesus as Israel's story lived again: the child called out of Egypt (Matthew 2:15), the passage through the waters, and now the wilderness. Israel was called God's son too: "Israel is My firstborn son" (Exodus 4:22). Moses explained what Israel's forty years were for: "Remember that these forty years the LORD your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart" (Deuteronomy 8:2). The hunger was a school, and its lesson was dependence: "He humbled you, and in your hunger He gave you manna to eat, which neither you nor your fathers had known, so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD" (Deuteronomy 8:3).

Israel failed the school. Hungry, they grumbled that they would have been better off in Egypt (Exodus 16:3). Thirsty, they "tested the LORD, saying, 'Is the LORD among us or not?'" (Exodus 17:7). At the foot of the mountain they bowed to a calf (Exodus 32). Now watch the Son in the same desert. Hungry, he is told to make bread for himself, and he answers with Deuteronomy 8:3. Set on the pinnacle of the temple and invited to throw himself down, with Psalm 91 quoted to him as a guarantee, he answers with Deuteronomy 6:16: "Do not put the Lord your God to the test" (Matthew 4:7). Shown the kingdoms of the world and offered them for one act of worship, he answers with Deuteronomy 6:13: "Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only" (Matthew 4:10). At each point where Israel failed, the Son trusted his Father.

Look again at the offers. The first would make his hunger his master and his sonship a tool for himself. The second bends a psalm about trust into a dare, which should give pause to anyone who knows a lot of verses. The third offers him the kingdoms he came to receive, without the cross he came to bear, and that last refusal will lead him to Jerusalem.

Lent's forty days remember his, though no one should try to repeat what he did. John Calvin, who opposed the Lenten fast of his day, argued that Christ didn't fast forty days to set an example for others to copy. Whatever a church decides about Lent, that much is a fair caution: his fast belongs to a singular moment, like Moses' on the mountain. Yet Jesus assumed his followers would fast. He said "When you fast" (Matthew 6:16), and he said that once the bridegroom was taken from them, "then they will fast" (Mark 2:20). A Christian fast is a short hunger turned toward God, the body's way of saying that we want him more than bread, kept quietly, without bargaining, and ending in a meal and thanksgiving.

Here we have to stand inside the story rather than above it. We are rarely tempted to turn stones into bread. We are tempted to make our comforts our masters, to demand that God prove himself on our schedule, and to reach good things, security and influence and approval, by bowing a little to whatever offers them. Churches know the third temptation well, and so do pastors. A small fast shows us what we have been living on; the empty hour where lunch used to be reveals how much of the day runs on small comforts.

The good news of this story is that he stood where we fall, and he stood there for us: "For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin" (Hebrews 4:15). Paul, writing about Israel's failures in the wilderness, adds a promise for ordinary days: "God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear" (1 Corinthians 10:13). The wilderness is where the Son showed that the Father's word is enough. Lent invites us a little way in, to find out whether we believe it.

scriptureStudy.note: "If You are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread" (Matthew 4:3). The tempter invites Jesus to use his sonship for himself. Jesus answers with Moses' words about the manna: "Man shall not live on bread alone" (Matthew 4:4).

The devil quotes Psalm 91:11-12, a psalm of trust, and turns it into a dare. Jesus answers, "Do not put the Lord your God to the test" (Matthew 4:7), from Deuteronomy 6:16, where Moses remembered Israel testing God at Massah.

"All this I will give You," he said, "if You will fall down and worship me" (Matthew 4:9). The kingdoms Jesus came to receive are offered without the cross. He refuses, and "angels came and ministered to Him" (Matthew 4:11).
"He humbled you, and in your hunger He gave you manna to eat" (Deuteronomy 8:3). The forty years were a school in dependence, and Moses says the lesson was that God's word is as necessary as bread.

"At once the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness" (Mark 1:12). Mark's account is brief and stark, and only Mark says, "He was with the wild animals" (Mark 1:13). Readers of Forty Days With Mark meet it on Ash Wednesday.

"We have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin" (Hebrews 4:15). Because his temptation was real, his sympathy is real, and the invitation follows: approach the throne of grace with confidence (Hebrews 4:16).

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the church's long argument about how to fast. The Didache, an early Christian manual probably from the late first or early second century, told believers to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays. The Shepherd of Hermas, from the second century, told those who fast to give what their food would have cost to a widow, an orphan, or someone in need. In the sixth century Benedict's Rule asked monks to add something in Lent to their usual measure of prayer and self-denial, to offer it with the joy of the Holy Spirit, and to tell their abbot what they planned and keep it with his blessing, since anything done without it would be counted presumption and vainglory. A thousand years later John Calvin commended fasting for three ends, to weaken the flesh, to prepare for prayer, and to humble ourselves before God when we confess our guilt, while attacking the Lenten fast of his day as superstition.

Each of these voices aims the fast at God, and several of them warn against a fast that turns into pride or into a rule. When the people of Bethel asked the priests and prophets whether to keep a fast they had kept for many years, God answered through Zechariah with a question: "was it really for Me that you fasted?" (Zechariah 7:5). A serious group should ask what keeps a fast honest, and whether a church can call people to fast without making it a law.
sessions.caseStudy:
Imagine that in the second week a college student announces that she plans to eat only one meal a day for all of Lent, and two others say they'll join her. One of them adds, laughing, that it will be good for her diet.

Don't praise the plan in front of everyone, and don't shame anyone for it either. Thank them for taking Lent seriously, read Matthew 6:16-18 and Isaiah 58:6-7, and ask the group what a fast is for. Repeat the health cautions for everyone, including that any fast longer than a day calls for a doctor's advice first and that a fast for weight is a diet, however devout it feels. Afterward, talk privately with the three, propose starting with one skipped meal a week instead, and if anything hints at a struggle with eating, encourage a conversation with a doctor or counselor.

Use this to show the room that zeal is a gift that needs counsel, as Benedict's monks told their abbot what they planned, and that a fast kept quietly and safely is no lesser fast.

memoryVerse.text: He humbled you, and in your hunger He gave you manna to eat, which neither you nor your fathers had known, so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.

sessions.title: Return
sessions.aim: To hear Joel's call to return as an invitation home that rests on God's own character, and to pray Psalm 51 as a real confession of real harm, so that repentance becomes a turning toward mercy and repair rather than a season of punishing ourselves.
sessions.summary:
Lent is often heard as forty days of feeling bad, or as a self-improvement plan with a religious label, and both miss what the prophets meant. Joel spoke to a land stripped bare by locusts and called the whole community to fast. Then came the word many churches read on Ash Wednesday: "'Yet even now,' declares the LORD, 'return to Me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning'" (Joel 2:12). God asks for torn hearts rather than torn clothes, and he gives the reason anyone would dare come back: "For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion" (Joel 2:13).

Psalm 51, which bears David's name, is set by its heading at the moment the prophet Nathan confronted David after he took Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and arranged Uriah's death. The psalm is a plea for mercy, a clean heart, and restored joy from a man who knows he can't pay for what he did: "For You do not delight in sacrifice, or I would bring it" (Psalm 51:16). The session distinguishes the sorrow that turns us toward God from the sorrow that only turns us in on ourselves, keeps in view the people our sin has harmed, and treats repentance as a turning toward home that shows in what we do next. For anyone taught to punish themselves, it is meant as good news.

keyScripture.why: "'Yet even now,' declares the LORD, 'return to Me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning'" (Joel 2:12). The call comes in the middle of a disaster and rests on God's character rather than the people's worthiness: "For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion" (Joel 2:13).

discussion.q: When you hear the word repentance, what do you feel, and where did you learn to feel it?
discussion.behind: Surface the inherited weight before you teach. Some people hear shame, a harsh parent, or a frightening sermon; some hear nothing at all, because the word has gone flat. Don't argue with anyone's answer. Those who grew up in churches that used guilt to control people may be wary of this whole session, and they have reasons. Go first.

discussion.q: Read Joel 2:12-14. What reason does God give for coming back, and what does the question "Who knows?" (Joel 2:14) add?
discussion.behind: The reason is God's character, in the words he spoke of himself to Moses after the golden calf (Exodus 34:6), not the people's performance. The question is humility, not bargaining: the people come back without a guarantee about the locusts but with confidence about who God is. Many churches read this passage on Ash Wednesday.

discussion.q: Read 2 Samuel 12:1-13. What does Nathan's story make David see that he couldn't see before? Then read Psalm 51:1-12. How does David's prayer differ from an apology meant to manage consequences?
discussion.behind: Let the room feel the turn when Nathan says, "You are that man!" (2 Samuel 12:7). David burned with anger at the rich man and couldn't see himself until the story showed him. Notice that Nathan names the harm: Uriah killed, his wife taken. Keep Bathsheba and Uriah in view; repentance that forgets the people harmed is not the repentance of Psalm 51.

discussion.q: Psalm 51:16-17 says God doesn't delight in sacrifice but won't despise "a broken and a contrite heart." What's the difference between a broken spirit and self-punishment? Why do we sometimes prefer punishing ourselves to being forgiven?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. A broken spirit is the end of pretending, not an injury we inflict to pay a debt. Self-punishment keeps us at the center and can never finish, because no amount of misery is ever enough. Talk privately with anyone who seems unable to stop condemning themselves, and suggest a pastor and a counselor.

discussion.q: Repentance in Scripture turns around and walks. Is there one place, a habit or a wrong done to someone, where returning to God would mean a concrete step this week?
discussion.behind: Don't ask anyone to confess anything to the group. Making amends should happen where it is safe and wise, often with a pastor's counsel, and never by seeking contact that would harm or frighten the person who was wronged. No one who has been abused is ever required to reconcile with the person who abused them. Anyone may pass.

objections.objection: Lent is a guilt machine. The church makes people feel worthless so it can sell them forgiveness.
objections.response: Churches have done exactly this, and the charge should be granted first. Guilt has been used to control people and keep them quiet, and some in this room were raised on it; their suspicion is earned, and the church should confess it rather than defend itself. But the guilt in Psalm 51 isn't manufactured. David took another man's wife and arranged his death, and a world with no room for guilt couldn't even say that what happened to Uriah was wrong. And the call to return rests on a mercy that comes before the confession: "For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger" (Joel 2:13). Real guilt named and forgiven sets people free. Guilt manufactured to control them is a sin against them, and the God of Joel has no part in it.

objections.objection: I was forgiven when I came to Christ. A whole season of repentance sounds like doubting grace, or trying to earn it again.
objections.response: The heart of this is right: forgiveness in Christ is complete, and no season can add to it, and any Lenten practice that tries to earn God's favor has misunderstood the gospel. But forgiven people still sin, and Scripture expects them to keep coming home: "If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves" (1 John 1:8), and "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins" (1 John 1:9). In 1517 Martin Luther began his Ninety-Five Theses by saying that when Jesus called people to repent, he meant the whole life of believers to be repentance. Returning isn't re-earning. It is how forgiven people live. Whether to give a season to it is a matter of freedom, and "each one should be fully convinced in his own mind" (Romans 14:5).

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What would it cost you to stop punishing yourself for something God has already forgiven, or to stop excusing something you have never honestly confessed?
sessions.practice: Pray Psalm 51:1-12 slowly each morning this week. On one evening, write down honestly one thing you need to turn from, and beside it write the description of God in Joel 2:13. If you have wronged someone and it is safe and wise to make it right, take one step toward repair; talk with a pastor first if you're unsure, and never seek contact that would harm or frighten the person you wronged. If you find you can't stop condemning yourself, tell a pastor or a counselor. That is part of returning too.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you are gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion, and you call us back even now. We confess that we have torn our garments and kept our hearts, that we have performed sorrow and avoided change, and that we have sometimes punished ourselves rather than trust your mercy. Show us our sin as Nathan showed David, and don't leave us there. Create in us clean hearts. Where we have harmed others, give us courage to make it right and wisdom to do it without harming them again. Restore to us the joy of your salvation, and turn us toward home. Amen.
reflection: What did I learn to feel when I hear the word repentance, and does it sound anything like Joel 2:13?
Where do I perform sorrow instead of turning, or punish myself instead of receiving mercy?
Is there someone I have wronged, and what would a safe and honest step toward repair look like?
sessions.teaching:
Lent is often heard in one of two ways. Some hear a self-improvement plan with a religious label: give up sugar, read more, and become a better version of yourself by Easter. Others hear forty days of feeling as bad as possible, as if misery could pay down a debt. Each holds a piece of the truth, since discipline is worth something and sorrow over sin is real, but neither is what the prophet Joel meant when he called his people to return.

Joel spoke to a land stripped bare: "What the devouring locust has left, the swarming locust has eaten" (Joel 1:4), wave after wave, until even the grain and drink offerings at the temple had run out. Scholars disagree about when Joel prophesied, and his message doesn't depend on the date. He called everyone in the land to "Consecrate a fast; proclaim a solemn assembly!" (Joel 1:14), and then came the word many churches read on Ash Wednesday: "'Yet even now,' declares the LORD, 'return to Me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning'" (Joel 2:12). The Hebrew word for return, shuv, is the Old Testament's ordinary word for repentance, and it means what it says: turn around and come back.

"So rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joel 2:13). In that world grief tore its clothes, and God asks for more than the outward sign. Then comes the reason anyone would dare come back: "For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. And He relents from sending disaster" (Joel 2:13). Those words echo the name God proclaimed to Moses (Exodus 34:6) just after Israel's betrayal at the golden calf. Joel stakes everything on God's character and nothing on the people's performance, and he leaves the outcome humbly open: "Who knows? He may turn and relent" (Joel 2:14). Everyone is called, the aged and the children, nursing infants, a bride and groom on their wedding day, and the priests weeping between the portico and the altar (Joel 2:16-17). Repentance in Joel is not only private, and the leaders aren't exempt.

Psalm 51 shows what such a turning sounds like from the inside. Its heading sets it at the moment "When Nathan the prophet came to him after his adultery with Bathsheba" (Psalm 51:1). King David saw another man's wife, sent for her, and took her, and when she was pregnant he arranged for her husband, Uriah, to die in battle. Nathan told him a parable about a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb, and David burned with anger until Nathan said, "You are that man!" (2 Samuel 12:7). Nathan named the harm plainly: "You put Uriah the Hittite to the sword and took his wife as your own" (2 Samuel 12:9). So when David prays, "Against You, You only, have I sinned" (Psalm 51:4), he isn't denying that Uriah and Bathsheba were wronged; he is standing before the court where every wrong is finally judged. Repentance that forgets the people we have harmed is not the repentance of this psalm, and the people our sin has hurt are never required to make us feel forgiven.

Listen to what David asks for: mercy "according to Your loving devotion" (Psalm 51:1), washing, a new heart, "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me" (Psalm 51:10), and joy, "Restore to me the joy of Your salvation" (Psalm 51:12). He never offers to punish himself, and the psalm says why: "For You do not delight in sacrifice, or I would bring it; You take no pleasure in burnt offerings. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit" (Psalm 51:16-17). A broken spirit is the end of pretending, not a wound we inflict. Paul drew the distinction sharply: "Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death" (2 Corinthians 7:10). Worldly sorrow turns in on itself and stays there; godly sorrow turns toward God and gets up.

We often prefer the theater of repentance to the thing itself: the public statement, the torn garment, the apology crafted to end the consequences. Some of us prefer punishing ourselves to being forgiven, because punishing ourselves keeps us in charge; it lets us pay, and it never has to end. Churches have encouraged both, and pastors aren't exempt from either.

In 1517 Martin Luther opened his Ninety-Five Theses by saying that when Jesus called people to repent, he meant the whole life of believers to be one of repentance. For churches that keep it, Lent is practice for that life, forty days of rehearsing the turn so that we can make it on an ordinary Tuesday. Whatever a church does with the season, repentance is the road home, and Joel insists that the God waiting at the end of it was gracious before anyone turned around.

scriptureStudy.note: "Return to Me with all your heart" (Joel 2:12). The call comes in the middle of the ruin and rests on God's character. "Who knows? He may turn and relent" (Joel 2:14) is humility, not a bargain.

"Gather the people, sanctify the congregation, assemble the aged, gather the children" (Joel 2:16). No one is too old, too young, or too happy to be included, and the priests weep for the people they serve.

"The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). God speaks his own name to Moses after the golden calf, and Joel stakes the call to return on these words.

"You are that man!" (2 Samuel 12:7). Nathan lets David condemn the rich man before showing him the mirror. David's answer is short and unguarded, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:13), and the consequences that follow are real.
"Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me" (Psalm 51:10). David asks for washing, a new heart, and restored joy. He offers no plan to pay for what he did.

"Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death" (2 Corinthians 7:10). Paul distinguishes the sorrow that turns toward God and changes a life from the sorrow that only turns inward and stays there.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the word confession, which has long meant more than one thing. Augustine's Confessions uses the Latin word in both its senses, the admission of sin and the praise of God, and the book does both throughout. A Christian confession of sin is spoken to someone, and the someone is gracious.

Then weigh the two failures the church keeps falling into. One is repentance that becomes payment, sorrow measured out to earn a release; Luther's Ninety-Five Theses, written in 1517 against the sale of indulgences, open by calling the whole life of believers one of repentance. The other is forgiveness that asks for no turning at all, which Dietrich Bonhoeffer in 1937 called cheap grace: grace without repentance, without discipleship, and without the cross. Most of us lean toward one of them by temperament. In 1930 T. S. Eliot, three years after he entered the Church of England, published Ash-Wednesday, a poem about turning that never pretends the turning is easy.

A serious group should ask which failure its own church is more prone to, and which one each person prefers. Then ask what it would look like for a congregation to return: to name a wrong it has done, to make what repair it can, and to trust the God of Joel 2:13 with the outcome.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose that in the third week a man the group looks to as steady says he has honestly never felt sorry for anything and wonders whether something is wrong with him. Later that evening a woman says she has spent every Lent since childhood sick with guilt and has been dreading this one.

Notice that Joel speaks to both. With him, read 2 Samuel 12:1-7 and ask the room why David could see the rich man's sin and not his own; most of us need a Nathan, and he may simply need time and honest friends. With her, read Joel 2:13 and Psalm 51:12, and say plainly that God's call to return is a call home, not a sentence to serve. Don't diagnose either of them. Afterward, talk with each privately, and if her guilt seems relentless, or tied to a fear of God that nothing relieves, encourage her to talk with a pastor and a counselor.

Use this to show the room that repentance is the same turning for everyone, whether the trouble is a numb conscience or a cruel one.

memoryVerse.text: Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from Your presence; take not Your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and sustain me with a willing spirit.

sessions.title: The Way of the Cross
sessions.aim: To read the call to take up the cross in its setting in Mark 8 and beside Isaiah's suffering servant, so that the room sees the cross first as what Christ carried for us and then as the shape of following him, and never as a demand to stay in harm.
sessions.summary:
Halfway through Mark's Gospel, Peter answers Jesus' question with "You are the Christ" (Mark 8:29), and Jesus begins to teach "that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and after three days rise again" (Mark 8:31). Peter rebukes him, and Jesus answers, "Get behind Me, Satan!" (Mark 8:33). Then he calls the crowd: "If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me" (Mark 8:34). In the Roman world a cross meant execution, the death the empire used to shame slaves and rebels. The phrase has shrunk in our mouths into a name for any annoyance, and it has been misused to tell people to stay where they were being hurt.

The session reads Mark 8 beside Isaiah 52:13-53:12, the song of the servant who "was pierced for our transgressions" (Isaiah 53:5), which the first Christians read as a portrait of Jesus. The cross is first what Christ carried for us, and only then the shape of our following, which means losing our lives for his sake and the gospel's and so saving them. It never means submitting to abuse. Readers of Forty Days With Mark meet this passage on the twentieth day, the middle of Lent.

keyScripture.why: After Peter's confession, Jesus "began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things" (Mark 8:31), and when Peter rebukes him, he calls the crowd: "If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me" (Mark 8:34). The call to follow is defined by his cross before it is applied to ours.

discussion.q: When have you heard someone say they had a cross to bear? What did they usually mean, and how does that compare with what a cross meant in the first century?
discussion.behind: Let the room notice how small the phrase has become: a bad knee, a difficult relative. Those burdens are real, and God cares about them, but in Jesus' world a man carrying a crossbeam was walking to his own execution. Don't mock anyone's use of the phrase. Simply let the first-century meaning come back.

discussion.q: Read Mark 8:27-33. Peter gets the title right and the plan wrong. Why do you think he rebuked Jesus, and why does Jesus answer so sharply?
discussion.behind: Peter wanted a Christ without a cross, which is understandable and very human. Jesus' answer echoes the wilderness: it is the same temptation, the kingdom without suffering, now in a friend's mouth. Help the room see that a church can confess the right creed and still rebuke Jesus for his plan.

discussion.q: Read Isaiah 53:3-6 aloud slowly. Which line stops you, and what does the song say the servant did for us?
discussion.behind: Let the text land before anyone explains it. Point out that the song speaks in the first person plural: "He was despised, and we esteemed Him not" (Isaiah 53:3). Be honest that many Jewish readers have understood the servant as Israel, while the church from its first days read him as Jesus (Acts 8:34-35), and don't let the discussion become a debate about theories of the atonement.

discussion.q: Jesus says, "whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it" (Mark 8:35). What would losing your life for his sake look like on an ordinary Tuesday, in your work, your family, your money, or your reputation?
discussion.behind: Push past heroic answers to ordinary ones: telling the truth when a lie would protect you, forgiving, serving someone who can't repay, letting go of the need to be noticed, speaking of Christ when it costs. Luke records that the cross is taken up "daily" (Luke 9:23). Answer first yourself, honestly and briefly.

discussion.q: This verse has been used to tell people to stay where they were being hurt. Why is that a misuse, and how would you say so to someone who had heard it?
discussion.behind: Say it plainly: taking up the cross never means staying in abuse. Jesus' cross was chosen for the good of others; abuse is someone else's sin against you, and Jesus told his disciples to flee persecution (Matthew 10:23). If anyone discloses that they aren't safe now, talk privately and connect them to help. If a child is being harmed, church leaders may be required by law to report it.

objections.objection: Take up your cross has been used to keep women in violent marriages and the poor in their place. Any teaching that glorifies suffering is dangerous.
objections.response: Grant this without hedging. The words have been used that way, by pastors and by churches, and harm done in Jesus' name is doubly wrong; the church should confess it. But the misuse contradicts the text. Jesus laid down his life by his own choice, to save others, and his call to take up the cross is never a reason to stay where you are being abused. Before his hour came he passed through a crowd that meant to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:29-30), and he told his followers, "When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next" (Matthew 10:23). Paul escaped Damascus in a basket (2 Corinthians 11:33). Again and again Scripture shows God's people getting out of danger when they can. If you are afraid of someone at home, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233, or 911 in an emergency.

objections.objection: A father who sends his son to die for other people's wrongs isn't loving. It sounds like the opposite of justice.
objections.response: The force of this should be felt, because some ways of telling the story have made God sound like an angry father punishing an unwilling son, and that picture is wrong. In the Christian confession the Son isn't a third party pulled in from outside: "God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ" (2 Corinthians 5:19), and Jesus says of his life, "No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord" (John 10:18). Christians describe what the cross accomplished with several of Scripture's images, sacrifice and substitution, ransom, victory over the powers, and a love that changes us, and faithful churches weigh them differently. All of them confess that "God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). You may still not believe it, but you aren't being asked to believe in a cruel father.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What are you most afraid you would lose if you followed Jesus all the way?
sessions.practice: Read Isaiah 52:13-53:12 aloud once this week, slowly, and Mark 8:27-38 on another day. Each evening, ask where you tried to save your life that day and where you lost a little of it for someone else's good. Choose one hidden act of service that no one will thank you for, and don't mention it. If this session stirred memories of being told to endure harm, talk with someone you trust. If you aren't safe at home, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233, or 911 in an emergency.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you didn't count equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied yourself and became obedient to death, even death on a cross. You were pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, and you carried what we could not carry. We confess that we have wanted the crown without the cross, for ourselves and for our churches, and that like Peter we have rebuked you for your plan. Forgive us. Teach us to lose our lives for your sake in small and hidden ways. Protect those who were told that their suffering was your will, and lead them to safety. Amen.
reflection: Have I made the cross small, a name for my inconveniences, or have I let it mean what Jesus meant?
Where am I like Peter, wanting Jesus without his plan?
What would losing my life for his sake look like this week, in one ordinary place?
sessions.teaching:
When people say they have a cross to bear, they usually mean a bad back, a difficult in-law, or a job they can't leave. Those burdens are real, and God cares about every one of them, but the phrase has shrunk. Rome used crucifixion above all for slaves, rebels, and those it most wanted to humiliate, and the New Testament scholar Martin Hengel gathered the ancient evidence that it was meant to shame as much as to kill. A man carrying a crossbeam through the streets was walking to his own death, and everyone watching knew it.

Mark sets the call at the turning point of his Gospel. In the villages around Caesarea Philippi, a city that bore the emperor's name, Peter answers Jesus' question, "You are the Christ" (Mark 8:29). Then Jesus "began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and after three days rise again" (Mark 8:31). Peter takes him aside and rebukes him, and we should be fair to Peter: no one who loves a friend wants to hear him predict his own death. But Jesus says in front of the others, "Get behind Me, Satan! For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men" (Mark 8:33). It is the wilderness again, the kingdom without the cross, offered this time by a friend.

Then Jesus calls the crowd: "If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me. For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it" (Mark 8:34-35). It is an invitation: if anyone wants to. To deny yourself is to stop being the center, the final authority on what your life is for; it has nothing to do with hating yourself or erasing the person God made. To take up the cross is to accept in advance that following him will cost you, and Luke records the saying with the word "daily" (Luke 9:23). Few of us will be asked to die for Christ. All of us will be asked, many times a week, to lose a little of our lives for someone else's good.

But before the cross is the shape of our following, it is what he carried for us. Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem from about 740 to at least 701 BC; who wrote the book's later chapters, and when, is debated, and the song of the servant in Isaiah 52:13-53:12 can be read with either view. It describes a servant "despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief" (Isaiah 53:3), and then tells the truth about him: "But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5). Many Jewish readers have understood the servant as Israel. The church read him as Jesus from its first days, when Philip "began with this very Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus" (Acts 8:35), and on the night of his arrest Jesus said, "this Scripture must be fulfilled in Me: 'And He was numbered with the transgressors'" (Luke 22:37).

The order matters. If we start with our cross, discipleship becomes a heroic project and the gospel becomes advice; if we stop with his, grace becomes cheap. In 1937 Dietrich Bonhoeffer gave that name, cheap grace, to forgiveness preached with no call to follow, and he set against it a costly grace, costly because it cost God the life of his Son and because it calls us to follow. He was executed at Flossenbürg in April 1945, weeks before the war in Europe ended.

One misuse has to be named plainly. These words have been used to tell abused wives to stay, to tell the poor to accept their lot, and to tell victims to keep quiet for a church's reputation. Every one of those uses turns the cross upside down: Jesus' cross was chosen, for the good of others, and abuse is someone else's sin against you. The call to follow Jesus is never a reason to stay in it.

What the way of the cross does mean is usually quieter: telling the truth when a lie would protect you, forgiving someone who hasn't earned it, serving people who can't repay you, and letting go of the need to be noticed. When his disciples quarreled over places of honor, Jesus told them, "whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant" (Mark 10:43), because he came "to give His life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). Churches want the Christ of Mark 8:29 without the suffering Son of Man of Mark 8:31, and so do pastors, and so do the rest of us. It was Peter's temptation before it was anyone else's.

In the same breath Jesus asks a question no amount of success can answer: "What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul?" (Mark 8:36). He asks it on the road to Jerusalem, where he will lose his own life for ours, and he asks us to walk that road with him.

scriptureStudy.note: "But what about you?" Jesus asked. "Who do you say I am?" (Mark 8:29). Peter's answer is right, and Jesus warns them not to tell anyone (Mark 8:30); what kind of Christ he is has not yet been made plain.

"He must be killed and after three days rise again" (Mark 8:31). Peter rebukes Jesus for his plan, and Jesus names the rebuke for what it is, a mind set on "the things of men" rather than "the things of God" (Mark 8:33).

"If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me" (Mark 8:34). The cost is stated before anyone answers: "What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul?" (Mark 8:36).

"Surely He took on our infirmities and carried our sorrows" (Isaiah 53:4). The onlookers thought God had struck him down for his own sins. The song corrects them: "the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:6).

"He was led like a lamb to the slaughter" (Isaiah 53:7). The servant is silent and buried with the wicked, yet "He will see the light of life and be satisfied" (Isaiah 53:11), and he "made intercession for the transgressors" (Isaiah 53:12).

"For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). Jesus answers a quarrel about greatness by pointing to his own death, and the many he dies for echoes the many of Isaiah 53:11-12.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the long conversation about what the cross accomplished. Anselm of Canterbury, in Why God Became Man, completed around 1098, argued that humanity owed God an honor it could not repay, and that only one who was both God and man could pay it. The Reformers spoke more directly of Christ bearing the penalty of sin in our place (Isaiah 53:5-6; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Many early Christian writers dwelt on the cross as a victory over sin, death, and the devil (Colossians 2:15), and others have stressed it as a revelation of love that changes those who see it (Romans 5:8). Each of these draws on Scripture, most traditions hold more than one, and faithful churches weigh them differently; this study leaves the weighing to your church's teaching.

Then weigh the call to follow. Thomas à Kempis's The Imitation of Christ, a fifteenth-century devotional classic, closes its second book with a chapter on the royal way of the holy cross. Bonhoeffer warned in 1937 that grace without following is cheap. Set beside them the history of the words' misuse, and ask how a church can call people to costly discipleship without ever making it a reason to remain in harm.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose that after the reading from Mark 8 a woman in your group says flatly that her mother stayed for thirty years with a husband who hit her, because a pastor told her it was her cross to bear. Then she goes quiet, and the room doesn't know where to look.

Don't hurry on, and don't explain the verse at her. Thank her for saying it. Say plainly, in front of everyone, that this was a misuse of Jesus' words, that taking up the cross never means staying where you are being hurt, and that the church owes her mother an apology. Don't ask for details. After the session, talk with her privately and ask whether she is safe now; if she is afraid of someone at home, give her the National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-7233, and help her make the call if she wants to. The care page /help/church-hurt may help with what she carries toward the church.

Use this to show the room that Christ's suffering was chosen for others, and that no one's abuse is a cross God asks them to carry.
