We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all.

sessions.title: The Darkest Week
sessions.aim: To walk through Mark 14 and 15 in portions, from the anointing at Bethany to the sealed tomb, watching who stays and who flees, and to end where the women ended, at the tomb on the Sabbath, with Easter morning still ahead.
sessions.summary:
Mark tells most of his story at a run, and then he slows down: the last six of his sixteen chapters cover a single week. This session reads Mark 14 and 15 in portions. A woman pours perfume on Jesus' head, and he says she has anointed his body for burial. At the Passover table he speaks of "My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many" (Mark 14:24). In Gethsemane he prays, "Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will" (Mark 14:36), while his friends sleep. He is arrested, "everyone deserted Him and fled" (Mark 14:50), and Peter denies him three times. Pilate hands him over to be crucified, and when he dies, a Roman centurion says, "Truly this man was the Son of God!" (Mark 15:39).

Mark pays close attention to who stays. The women are "watching from a distance" (Mark 15:40), and two of them see where the body is laid. The session ends there on purpose. Mark says nothing about Saturday, but Luke says the women "rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment" (Luke 23:56). The study leaves the group at a sealed tomb, with Easter morning ahead and not yet come, and names the day between the death and the resurrection as a day the church keeps for everyone still waiting.

keyScripture.why: "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Mark 15:34). Jesus prays Psalm 22 in the dark and dies, a centurion confesses him, Joseph of Arimathea buries him, and "Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph saw where His body was placed" (Mark 15:47). It is the Holy Saturday reading in Forty Days With Mark.

discussion.q: Read Mark 14:3-9. Why do some at the table call the woman's gift a waste, and why does Jesus say that what she has done will be told wherever the gospel is preached?
discussion.behind: Let the room feel the extravagance and the scolding. When Jesus says the poor will always be with them (Mark 14:7), he echoes Deuteronomy 15:11, a command to open your hand to the poor, so he isn't dismissing them. Notice what comes next, as Judas goes to the chief priests.

discussion.q: Read Mark 14:32-42. What do you notice about how Jesus prays in Gethsemane, and about the friends who fall asleep?
discussion.behind: Jesus is "deeply troubled and distressed" (Mark 14:33); he asks for the cup to pass and submits to his Father's will, so honest prayer and surrender belong together. His friends sleep, and he still speaks of them with understanding: "the spirit is willing, but the body is weak" (Mark 14:38).

discussion.q: "Then everyone deserted Him and fled" (Mark 14:50), and Peter denies him three times. Where do you see yourself in the disciples' fear? What do Mark 14:28 and Mark 16:7 tell you Jesus had planned for them?
discussion.behind: Let people own the fear without groveling. Then point to the grace prepared in advance: before they fled, Jesus promised to go ahead of them into Galilee (Mark 14:28), and on Easter morning the message is for "His disciples and Peter" (Mark 16:7). Peter is named. The failure is real, and it is not final.

discussion.q: Read Mark 15:33-41. Who confesses Jesus at his death, and who is still there? Why might it matter that Mark names the women who stayed?
discussion.behind: The centurion is the first human being in Mark's story to call Jesus the Son of God; apart from Mark's own first line (Mark 1:1), only the voice from heaven and the unclean spirits have said it. The women had followed Jesus from Galilee and stayed when the men fled; they saw him die, saw where he was buried, and came to the tomb on Sunday. Mark names them, and his first readers could know exactly who had seen.

discussion.q: The study ends at the tomb on Saturday. What does it mean to you that there is a day in the Christian story between the death and the resurrection? Who do you know who is living in that day right now?
discussion.behind: Don't rush to Sunday. Some in the room are in a long Saturday of grief, illness, or unanswered prayer; let them say so, and don't fix it. Invite the group to Good Friday and Easter worship if your church holds them, and point them to the reading for Easter morning, Mark 16:1-8.

objections.objection: These stories were written decades later by believers with a cause. Why trust any of it?
objections.response: It's the right question to ask. Most scholars date Mark to the late 60s or early 70s, a generation after the events, and Mark wrote as a believer with a purpose; his first line says so. But notice what kind of story he tells. The men who led the early church come off badly: they sleep, they flee, and Peter curses and swears that he never knew Jesus. The witnesses of the death, the burial, and the empty tomb are women, in a world that often discounted a woman's word. Many historians give weight to details like these, which embarrass the people telling them and so are unlikely to have been invented. Pilate governed Judea from about AD 26 to 36, and early in the second century the Roman historian Tacitus recorded that Christ was executed under him. The study of the resurrection, /studyguides/resurrection, takes up the larger question.

objections.objection: If Jesus cried, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Mark 15:34), then either he lost his faith or God really did abandon him.
objections.response: Few sentences in the Gospels are harder to hear, and this one shouldn't be explained away. But it is a prayer, addressed to "My God," and it is the first line of Psalm 22, a psalm that bears David's name and moves from abandonment to trust: the LORD "has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help" (Psalm 22:24). Christians read the cry in more than one way. Some stress that he truly bore the abandonment that sin deserves; others, that by praying the psalm's first line he claimed its whole arc in trust; many hold both. On every reading he keeps praying, and he prays Scripture. If you have prayed that line in your own dark, you were praying with him.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Which person in Mark's account are you most like this year: the woman with the jar, the friends asleep in the garden, Peter by the fire, the women watching from a distance, or Joseph asking for the body?
sessions.practice: This Holy Week, read one portion of Mark 14 and 15 each day, or follow the last days of the Forty Days With Mark plan, /plans#lent-with-mark, which reaches the burial on Saturday. On Friday, if you can, set aside an hour of quiet, keep a simple fast within the health cautions from the second session, or go to your church's Good Friday service. On Saturday, read Mark 15:42-47 and Luke 23:54-56, and don't hurry past the day. On Easter morning, read Mark 16:1-8, and if you can, share a meal with others.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you were anointed for burial by a woman the others scolded, betrayed by a friend, deserted by the rest, and denied by Peter at a fire. You prayed in the garden for the cup to pass, and you drank it. You cried out to your God in the dark, and you died. We have slept when you asked us to watch, and we have warmed ourselves at other fires. Forgive us. We leave you tonight where the women left you, in a tomb cut out of the rock, with a stone across the door. Keep us through the Sabbath, and when it is over, bring us early to the tomb. Amen.
reflection: Where have I slept, fled, or warmed myself at the fire when I could have stayed near Jesus?
What does it mean to me that Jesus prayed Psalm 22 on the cross?
Who do I know who is living in a long Saturday, and how can I keep them company without hurrying them?
sessions.teaching:
Mark tells most of his Gospel at a run; one of his favorite words, usually translated at once or immediately, tumbles the scenes one into the next. Then he slows down. The last six of his sixteen chapters cover a single week, and by the end he is marking the hours: "It was the third hour when they crucified Him" (Mark 15:25).

It begins with a gift. In Bethany a woman breaks an alabaster jar of perfume and pours it on Jesus' head, and some at the table scold her for the waste. Jesus defends her: "She has done what she could to anoint My body in advance of My burial" (Mark 14:8). Mark never gives her name, yet Jesus promises that what she did "will also be told in memory of her" (Mark 14:9). In the next verse Judas goes to the chief priests, and extravagant love and calculated betrayal sit side by side.

At the Passover table Jesus says of the cup, "This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many" (Mark 14:24), the many of Isaiah's servant song. Then, in Gethsemane, the Son who trusted his Father in the wilderness trusts him again in a garden. He says, "My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death" (Mark 14:34), and he prays, "Abba, Father ... all things are possible for You. Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will" (Mark 14:36). Mark keeps the Aramaic word for father. The prayer holds honest anguish and real surrender together, and his friends sleep through it.

Then the arrest, and a sentence Mark lets stand without comment: "Then everyone deserted Him and fled" (Mark 14:50). Peter follows at a distance into the high priest's courtyard and warms himself by the fire, and when a servant girl recognizes him he denies Jesus three times, the last time with curses. The rooster crows, and "he broke down and wept" (Mark 14:72). Yet before any of this Jesus had told them, "after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee" (Mark 14:28). The restoration was prepared before the fall.

The chief priests hand Jesus over to Pilate, who knows they have done it out of envy (Mark 15:10), and Pilate, "wishing to satisfy the crowd" (Mark 15:15), hands him over to be crucified. Here the church has to be careful and honest at once. For centuries Christians read this chapter as an accusation against the Jewish people, and Holy Week became an occasion for contempt and violence against Jews. That was a grave sin, and the church has repented of the charge. In 1965 the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate said that the passion cannot be charged against all Jews then living or against Jews today, and other churches have said the same. Jesus was a Jew, and so were the disciples who fled and the women who stayed. Mark spreads the failure widely: religious leaders moved by envy, a governor moved by expedience, a crowd easily stirred, soldiers who mock, and friends who run. The Roman Catechism of 1566 taught that sinners of every age, and Christians above all, are the authors of Christ's sufferings. That is where we stand in this story.

Mark is spare about the suffering. "And they crucified Him" (Mark 15:24) is nearly all he says of the act itself. The mockers say, "He saved others, but He cannot save Himself!" (Mark 15:31), truer than they knew; to save others he would not save himself. At the ninth hour Jesus cries out the first line of Psalm 22, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Mark 15:34), praying Scripture in the dark, a psalm that ends in praise and promises that "all who go down to the dust will kneel before Him" (Psalm 22:29). He breathes his last, the veil of the temple is torn from top to bottom, and a Roman centurion says, "Truly this man was the Son of God!" (Mark 15:39).

Then Mark turns to the women: "And there were also women watching from a distance" (Mark 15:40). He names them, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome, women who had followed Jesus in Galilee. The men have fled, and the women stay. Joseph of Arimathea, a council member "who himself was waiting for the kingdom of God" (Mark 15:43), asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in linen, lays it in a tomb cut out of the rock, and rolls a stone against the entrance. "Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph saw where His body was placed" (Mark 15:47). They are witnesses of the death and the burial, and on the first day of the week they will be witnesses of the empty tomb.

Mark says nothing about Saturday. Luke says only, "And they rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment" (Luke 23:56). The Apostles' Creed confesses that he was crucified, dead, and buried, and that he descended into hell, a clause whose older sense is that he went to the dead; Christians read it in more than one way, and at the least it guards the truth that he really died. This study ends here on purpose. Many people live a long time in a Saturday, after a death or a diagnosis or a prayer that seems to go unanswered, and the day the church remembers between the cross and the empty tomb belongs to them too.

Easter morning will come. "When the Sabbath was over" (Mark 16:1), the women will go to anoint a body and find an empty tomb, and that is the reading for Easter Sunday. Tonight we stop where they stopped, at the stone, and we keep the Sabbath with them.

scriptureStudy.note: "She has done a beautiful deed to Me" (Mark 14:6). While others at the table see only waste, Jesus says the unnamed woman has anointed his body for burial (Mark 14:8), and he promises that her deed will be told "in memory of her" (Mark 14:9).

"Yet not what I will, but what You will" (Mark 14:36). In the garden Jesus asks honestly for the cup to pass and then surrenders to his Father. His friends sleep, and he speaks of their weakness with understanding (Mark 14:38).

"I do not know this man of whom you speak!" (Mark 14:71). Peter's denial grows from evasion to oaths. When the rooster crows, "he broke down and wept" (Mark 14:72). On Easter morning the young man in white at the tomb names him (Mark 16:7).

"Truly this man was the Son of God!" (Mark 15:39). After the darkness, the cry of Psalm 22, and the torn veil, a Gentile soldier at an execution makes the confession Mark announced in his first line (Mark 1:1).

"And there were also women watching from a distance" (Mark 15:40). The women who followed from Galilee stay when the men have fled, and two of them see "where His body was placed" (Mark 15:47), so they know where to come on the first day of the week.
"And they rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment" (Luke 23:56). Luke gives Holy Saturday one sentence. The spices are ready, the tomb is closed, and the women keep the Sabbath.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the ways the church has kept this week, and the ways it has failed in keeping it. Late in the fourth century the pilgrim Egeria described the Christians of Jerusalem moving from place to place through the days before Easter, reading the accounts of the passion where the events were remembered. In many early churches new believers were baptized at Easter, a practice that echoes Paul's words: "We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death" (Romans 6:4).

The church has also failed this week badly. For centuries Holy Week preaching and plays stirred contempt for Jews, and Christians committed violence against their Jewish neighbors in these very days. The Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) is short enough for a group to read together, and its fourth section answers the charge directly. Christians also read the creed's line about the descent differently: some hold that Christ proclaimed his victory to the dead (1 Peter 3:18-19), some that the line confesses that he truly lay in death until the third day, and some, following John Calvin, read it as the agony he bore on the cross. A serious group should ask how to read the passion so that it humbles every reader rather than accusing someone else.
sessions.caseStudy:
Imagine that in the last session a man who has come every week says that Easter has been hard for him since his wife died in the spring two years ago. The music and the lilies felt like being told to cheer up, and he asks whether it would be wrong to skip Easter this year.

Don't argue with him, and don't promise that this Easter will feel different. Read Luke 23:56 and Mark 16:8 aloud. The women rested on the Sabbath with their grief, and on Easter morning they fled the tomb "trembling and bewildered" (Mark 16:8). The first Easter wasn't cheerful. It was overwhelming. Tell him he is welcome to sit near the back, or to read Mark 16:1-8 at home and come another week, and that the resurrection doesn't depend on what he feels. Ask whether you can check on him on Easter afternoon, and mention the care page /help/grief.

Use this to show the room that Easter answers death without erasing grief, and that the church can make room for people who arrive at the empty tomb still weeping.

memoryVerse.text: “Abba, Father,” He said, “all things are possible for You. Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will.”

leaderPrimer:
Your room may hold people who have kept Lent all their lives and people from churches that never did, a skeptic who came out of curiosity, someone who buried a husband or wife this winter, someone with a long and private struggle with food, and someone with diabetes who wants to fast with everyone else. The hazards of leading this study are quiet ones: turning Lent into a contest over who gave up the most, a self-improvement program with a religious label, or a season of guilt. Keep everything voluntary and quiet. Don't count who is fasting, don't promise what a fast will get, and don't let anyone be shamed for eating. Say from the front, more than once, that no one is less faithful for fasting from something other than food.

Know the health cautions before the first session, and say them plainly, because the first session's practice invites people to choose a fast. Anyone should talk with a doctor before fasting from food if they have had an eating disorder or a long struggle with food, if they have diabetes or another medical condition or take regular medication, if they are pregnant or nursing or under eighteen, or if fasting has become about weight or control. A beginner's fast is one meal, never a fast from water; anyone who feels faint, dizzy, or unwell should eat, and anyone considering a fast longer than a day should see a doctor first. Someone who drinks heavily every day shouldn't give up alcohol for Lent without a doctor's help, because stopping suddenly can bring on a dangerous withdrawal; a seizure or hallucinations call for 911. The care page /help/fasting gathers these cautions. Nothing in this guide is medical advice.

Some sessions will touch wounds. Ash Wednesday's words and the passion narratives can land hard on the grieving, the seriously ill, and anyone who has known violence; let anyone step out, never call on anyone, and don't press. For someone already in despair, hearing that we are dust can sound like a verdict on their worth. Never say it without the other half of Psalm 103, the Father's compassion for the dust, and watch for anyone who speaks of not wanting to live. The third session takes up repentance, which some will hear as permission to punish themselves; if someone can't stop condemning themselves, talk with them privately and suggest a pastor and a counselor. The fourth takes up the call to take up the cross, words that have been used to tell people to stay where they were being hurt. Say plainly that it never means that: safety comes before reconciliation, and no one should ever be counseled to stay in danger. The fifth reads the passion, which Christians long used to accuse the Jewish people; the teaching says plainly that the church has repented of that charge, and if anyone in the room repeats it, correct it kindly and clearly.

Never ask anyone to disclose danger, abuse, or thoughts of suicide in the group. If it comes out anyway, stop, thank the person, and talk with them privately as soon as you can. If someone speaks of not wanting to live, take it seriously every time: stay with them and call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, together, or call 911 if anyone is in immediate danger. If someone is afraid of a person at home, point them to the National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788. If a child is being harmed, the child's safety comes first; church leaders may be mandated reporters of child abuse and neglect, the laws vary by state, and this guide can't give legal advice, so learn your obligations before the study begins. Set the rule of confidentiality at the first meeting with its limits: you won't keep secret anything that puts someone in danger.

Several questions in this study are open among faithful Christians, and the guide deliberately leaves them open. The first is whether to keep Lent and the church year at all. Some churches receive the season as a gift from the early church, a yearly walk through the life of Christ rooted in the early fast before Easter and the preparation of new believers for baptism. They point to Paul's word that whoever observes a special day does so to the Lord (Romans 14:6), and the comfort they find is a shared rhythm that holds you on the days you can't hold yourself. Other churches hold that believers are free of any season Scripture doesn't command. They have watched church customs harden into rules and merit, and they point to the letter to the Colossians, which tells believers not to let anyone judge them about a feast, because such things are a shadow and the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16-17). The comfort they find is freedom: nothing on a calendar can add to what Christ has done, and every Lord's Day celebrates the resurrection. To both, Paul says neither may belittle or judge the other, "for God has accepted him" (Romans 14:3). Faithful churches differ here, and James Bell's own landing is not given in this guide. The same is true of whether to receive ashes on Ash Wednesday, of how to weigh the Bible's images for what the cross accomplished, and of how to read the creed's line about the descent. State each view fairly, let people disagree and remain brothers and sisters, and leave the rest to your church's teaching.

Lead from inside. You aren't the best faster in the room and don't need to be; keep a small Lent of your own, and be honest about how it goes. The study ends at a sealed tomb on Saturday, on purpose. Invite the group to Good Friday and Easter worship if your church holds them, and after Easter, the study of the resurrection, /studyguides/resurrection, is a natural next step.

faq.q: What is Lent, and where did it come from?
faq.a: Lent is the forty days before Easter. In Western churches it begins on Ash Wednesday, forty-six days before Easter, because the Sundays, traditionally feast days, aren't counted; Eastern Orthodox churches begin their Great Lent on a Monday and usually keep Easter on a different date. The Bible never commands Lent. Near the end of the second century Irenaeus of Lyon describes Christians fasting before Easter, some for a day and some for longer, and by the fourth century many churches kept a forty-day season, closely tied to preparing new believers for baptism at Easter.

faq.q: Do Christians have to keep Lent?
faq.a: The Bible doesn't require it, and faithful Christians disagree about whether to keep it at all. The Roman Catholic Church asks most adults to fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday; many churches mark the season and leave the fast to each person; others don't keep it. Those who keep it receive the church year as a gift, a yearly walk through the life of Christ, and say that a season can teach without saving anyone: "He who observes a special day does so to the Lord" (Romans 14:6). Those who don't keep it hold that believers are free of any season Scripture doesn't command, and they have seen church customs harden into a law or turn into a show; the letter to the Colossians tells believers not to let anyone judge them by what they eat "or with regard to a feast" (Colossians 2:16). To both, Paul says that neither may belittle or judge the other, "for God has accepted him" (Romans 14:3). This study doesn't settle the question.

faq.q: Our church doesn't keep Lent. Can we still use this study?
faq.a: Yes. Nothing in it requires you to keep a church season, observe Ash Wednesday, or fast. Its passages belong to every church's Bible, from Genesis 3 and Psalm 51 to the last chapters of Mark, and the case for not keeping Lent is stated as fairly as the case for keeping it.

faq.q: Is it safe for me to fast?
faq.a: Start with your health. Talk with a doctor before you fast from food if you've had an eating disorder or a long struggle with food, if you have diabetes or another medical condition or take regular medication, if you're pregnant or nursing or under eighteen, or if fasting has become about weight or control. You can fast from something else instead, and no one is less faithful for it. Otherwise, begin with one meal, keep drinking water, and eat if you feel faint or unwell. Talk with a doctor before any fast longer than a day, and if you drink heavily every day, see a doctor before giving up alcohol for Lent. The care page /help/fasting says more. This isn't medical advice.

faq.q: What should I give up for Lent?
faq.a: Choose something you'll miss every day, so that its absence keeps reminding you why: a meal, meat, alcohol, social media, a nightly show. Don't give up a sin for Lent; give that up for good. Don't choose anything that would harm you or the people who depend on you. If food is hard for you, fast from something else, and if you drink heavily every day, talk with a doctor before you stop. Many people also take something up, such as the printable Forty Days With Mark plan, /plans#lent-with-mark, a time of prayer, or a gift to the hungry from what they save.

faq.q: What is Ash Wednesday, and do I have to receive ashes?
faq.a: It is the first day of Lent in Western churches, when many churches mark each forehead with ash, often in the sign of a cross, with words drawn from Genesis 3:19 about returning to dust, or with Jesus' call to repent and believe the gospel (Mark 1:15). In Scripture ashes went with grief and repentance (Daniel 9:3; Jonah 3:6). Some Christians think the practice sits uneasily with Jesus' warning not to show your fasting (Matthew 6:16-18); those who keep it answer that the ash is a shared confession, not a display. Receiving ashes is a matter of freedom.

faq.q: Why forty days, and are Sundays part of Lent?
faq.a: Scripture often uses forty for seasons of testing and preparation: Moses on the mountain forty days and nights (Exodus 34:28), Elijah's forty days to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8), Israel's forty years in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 8:2), and Jesus' forty-day fast before he began to preach (Matthew 4:2). Lent's forty days remember his, though no one should try to repeat what he did. The Sundays aren't counted, because every Sunday celebrates the resurrection, and many people set their fast aside on them; that is why, in Western churches, Lent begins on Ash Wednesday, forty-six days before Easter.

faq.q: Isn't Lent just self-improvement with a religious label?
faq.a: It can become that, and the criticism deserves a hearing. A fast that is really a diet, a test of willpower, or a way to feel better about ourselves by Easter has bent back toward the self, and Jesus' warning about fasting to be seen applies (Matthew 6:16-18). God put the same question to his people through Zechariah: "was it really for Me that you fasted?" (Zechariah 7:5). In Scripture a fast is hunger turned toward God and pointed at the neighbor; the fast God chose is "to share your bread with the hungry" (Isaiah 58:7).

faq.q: I'm not a Christian. Is this study for me?
faq.a: Yes, if you're willing to sit with the questions. The first session begins with something every person shares, that we will die, and takes seriously the argument that religion is a way of coping with death. No one will ask you to pretend to believe, to fast, or to receive ashes, only to read old and serious texts honestly and weigh what Christians claim about them. The study of the resurrection, /studyguides/resurrection, weighs the central claim directly.

faq.q: Why does the study end on Saturday instead of Easter?
faq.a: Because that is where the women were left. Mark's account of the burial ends with two of the women seeing where the body was laid (Mark 15:47), and Luke says that "they rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment" (Luke 23:56). Ending there lets the group feel the weight of the day before Easter, and it makes room for people living in a long Saturday of their own. The Forty Days With Mark plan reads Mark 16:1-8 on Easter morning, and the study of the resurrection, /studyguides/resurrection, is a natural next step.

faq.q: Does taking up the cross mean I should stay where I'm being hurt?
faq.a: No. Jesus' cross was chosen, for the good of others, in obedience to his Father; abuse is someone else's sin against you. Jesus told his followers to flee persecution (Matthew 10:23), and Paul escaped Damascus in a basket (2 Corinthians 11:33). Jesus' call to follow him is never a reason to stay where you are being abused, and anyone who told you otherwise misused his words. If you are afraid of someone at home, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 or text START to 88788, and call 911 if you are in immediate danger.

faq.q: Can families and teenagers keep Lent with this study?
faq.a: Teenagers can take part in the discussion, and no question requires anyone to share. Anyone under eighteen should talk with a parent and a doctor before fasting from food, and can fast from something else instead: a phone, a game, a favorite show. For households, How to Keep Lent and Easter as a Family, /how-tos/fam-how-to-keep-lent-and-easter-as-a-family, has ideas that work with children.

timeline.event: David reigns over Israel. Psalm 51 and Psalm 103 bear his name; the heading of Psalm 51 sets it after the prophet Nathan confronted him over Bathsheba and Uriah (2 Samuel 12).
Isaiah son of Amoz prophesies in Jerusalem. The book that bears his name contains the song of the suffering servant (Isaiah 52:13-53:12); when and by whom its later chapters were written is debated.

Jesus is baptized by John and led into the wilderness for forty days (Mark 1:9-13). His ministry ends in Jerusalem at Passover, when he is crucified under Pontius Pilate, governor of Judea from about AD 26 to 36.
Most scholars date Mark's Gospel to these years, and early tradition links Mark with the preaching of Peter.

timeline.date: Late first or early second century
timeline.event: The Didache, an early Christian manual, tells believers to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays and to fast before a baptism.

When Victor, bishop of Rome, tries to cut off the churches of Asia Minor over the date of Easter, Irenaeus of Lyon reminds him that Christians fast before Easter for different lengths of time, and that the difference confirms their agreement in the faith.
The Council of Nicaea, in its fifth canon, directs that one of a province's two yearly synods of bishops meet before the forty days (in Greek, tessarakoste), naming the season without explaining it.
The pilgrim Egeria, visiting Jerusalem, describes how the church there keeps the days before Easter, including a procession with branches from the Mount of Olives on the Sunday before Easter.
Benedict's Rule asks each monk in Lent to add something to the usual measure of prayer and self-denial, to tell his abbot what he plans, and to keep it with the joy of the Holy Spirit.
Martin Luther opens his Ninety-Five Theses by saying that when Jesus called people to repent, he meant the whole life of believers to be one of repentance.

In Lent, sausages are served and eaten at the Zurich house of the printer Christoph Froschauer, and Huldrych Zwingli, preacher at the Grossmünster, defends those who ate them in a sermon on Christian freedom in food.
The Westminster Assembly's Directory for the Public Worship of God holds that no day but the Lord's Day is commanded to be kept holy, yet it still gives directions for days of public fasting.

The Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate states that the passion of Christ cannot be charged against all Jews then living or against Jews today, repudiating a charge that long stained the keeping of Holy Week.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for coming. Over these weeks we'll walk from Ash Wednesday toward Easter, and first, a few things. What is said in this room stays in this room, with one exception: if someone is in danger of harming themselves or someone else, or a child is being harmed, I won't keep that secret, and I may be required to get help. No one here has to share anything; you're welcome to listen the whole time. Lent is kept quietly. No one will ask what you've given up, no one is keeping score, and no one is less faithful for fasting from something other than food. If you plan to fast from food, please read the health cautions in your handout first, and never go without water. Some of us have kept Lent all our lives and some of us never have, and both are welcome. None of us stands above what we'll talk about: death, temptation, repentance, the cross. Tonight we are looking at this together: ________. Let me read our passage, and then we'll sit with it before anyone says anything. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, off the page and into the places where Lent is actually kept: the kitchen at lunchtime, the phone late at night, the conversation we've been avoiding. That is where this either matters or it doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We'll stop there, even though nothing is finished, because Lent isn't finished in an evening. Try the practice if you can; if you can only manage the reflection question, that counts. If you're fasting, keep it quiet and keep it safe, and if you feel unwell, eat. If you're in danger or thinking about ending your life, call or text 988, or 911 in an emergency, and please tell me. What was said here stays here. Let me pray for us before we go.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Written about 397 to 400 as a prayer to God that confesses both sin and praise. It opens with the heart restless until it rests in God, tells in its fourth book of the death of a close friend, and in its eighth of Augustine's conversion in a garden in Milan in 386. Sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: On the Incarnation
bibliography.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
bibliography.note: A fourth-century argument that the Word of God took a human body so that, by dying and rising, he might undo the corruption and death that came through sin; Athanasius points to Christians who no longer fear death as they once did as evidence that death has been overcome. Session 1.

bibliography.title: The Rule of Saint Benedict
bibliography.author: Benedict of Nursia
bibliography.note: A sixth-century rule for monks. It counts keeping death daily before one's eyes among the tools of the spiritual life, and its chapter on Lent asks each monk to add something to the usual measure of prayer and self-denial, to tell his abbot what he plans, and to await Easter with the joy of spiritual longing. Sessions 1 and 2.

bibliography.title: Institutes of the Christian Religion
bibliography.author: John Calvin
bibliography.note: In the final edition of 1559, book four, chapter twelve, on the discipline of the church, Calvin commends fasting for three ends, to weaken the flesh, to prepare for prayer, and to humble ourselves before God in confessing our guilt. In the same chapter he criticizes the Lenten fast of his day as superstition and argues that Christ's forty days were not meant as an example to copy. A Reformation voice against keeping Lent that still commends fasting. Session 2.

bibliography.title: The Directory for the Public Worship of God
bibliography.author: The Westminster Assembly
bibliography.note: Prepared by the Westminster Assembly in the 1640s. It holds that no day but the Lord's Day is commanded to be kept holy under the gospel and that festival days are not to be continued, and it still gives directions for days of public fasting. The case against keeping holy days, from the Puritan and Presbyterian side of the Reformation.

bibliography.title: The Cost of Discipleship
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Published in German in 1937 as Nachfolge. It names cheap grace, forgiveness preached without repentance, discipleship, or the cross, and sets against it a costly grace that calls a person to follow Jesus in concrete obedience. Sessions 3 and 4.

bibliography.title: Great Lent: Journey to Pascha
bibliography.author: Alexander Schmemann
bibliography.note: An Orthodox priest and teacher, first published in 1969, describes Lent as the church's preparation for Pascha, the feast of the resurrection, and calls the season's mood a bright sadness. The case for keeping the season, from the Eastern church.

bibliography.title: Ancient-Future Time: Forming Spirituality through the Christian Year
bibliography.author: Robert E. Webber
bibliography.note: An evangelical theologian commends the Christian year, from Advent to Pentecost, as a way of being formed by the life of Christ rather than by the culture's calendar. The case for keeping the church year, from a Protestant voice.

bibliography.title: Celebration of Discipline
bibliography.author: Richard J. Foster
bibliography.note: First published in 1978. It describes twelve classical disciplines of the Christian life, fasting among them, as means by which we place ourselves before God so that he can change us. Session 2.

bibliography.title: The Denial of Death
bibliography.author: Ernest Becker
bibliography.note: A cultural anthropologist argues that much human striving is a flight from the knowledge of death, organized into projects meant to make us feel we will last. Published in 1973 and awarded the Pulitzer Prize in 1974. Not a Christian book; tested against Scripture in session 1.

bibliography.title: The Cross of Christ
bibliography.author: John Stott
bibliography.note: Published in 1986. It argues that the cross is the center of the Christian faith and that God, in Christ, substituted himself for sinners, holding together the gravity of sin and the greatness of God's love. Session 4.

bibliography.title: Crucifixion in the Ancient World and the Folly of the Message of the Cross
bibliography.author: Martin Hengel
bibliography.note: Published in English in 1977. A New Testament scholar gathers the ancient evidence that crucifixion was a deliberately degrading death, inflicted above all on slaves, violent criminals, and rebels, and shows why a crucified Messiah sounded like folly to the ancient world (1 Corinthians 1:23). Session 4.

bibliography.title: The Crucifixion: Understanding the Death of Jesus Christ
bibliography.author: Fleming Rutledge
bibliography.note: Published in 2015. It argues that the crucifixion, a death of utmost shame, is the center of the Christian proclamation, and gathers the Bible's many images for what the cross accomplished without letting one silence the others. Sessions 4 and 5.

furtherReading: Great Lent, Alexander Schmemann, for readers who want to see the season from inside the Orthodox church, as a preparation for the joy of Easter.
Institutes of the Christian Religion, John Calvin, book four, chapter twelve, for a Reformation case for fasting without keeping Lent.
Celebration of Discipline, Richard J. Foster, for a wider view of the practices of the Christian life, fasting among them.
The Cross of Christ, John Stott, for readers ready to think hard about what the cross accomplished.
The Cost of Discipleship, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for anyone who suspects that grace without following is not the grace of the New Testament.

glossary.definition: The forty days before Easter, kept by many churches as a season of prayer, fasting, and giving, and not kept by others. Its forty days remember Jesus' forty in the wilderness.
The first day of Lent in Western churches, when many churches mark foreheads with ash and speak words drawn from Genesis 3:19, or Jesus' call to repent and believe the gospel (Mark 1:15).
The day before Ash Wednesday. Its name comes from an old English word for hearing confession and giving absolution, and in many places it became a day for using up rich foods before the fast.
Going without food, or something else, for a time, as hunger turned toward God, joined in Scripture to prayer and to care for the hungry.
Giving to the poor. With prayer and fasting it is one of the three practices Jesus names in Matthew 6:1-18, and the three have long been kept together in Lent.
Turning from sin and returning to God. The Old Testament's ordinary word for it, shuv, means to turn around and come back; the New Testament's word, metanoia, means a change of mind.
In Scripture, the desert place of testing and provision, where Israel wandered forty years and Jesus fasted forty days.
A person being taught the faith before baptism. In the early church many were baptized at Easter, and Lent grew partly as their final preparation, with the whole church fasting alongside them.
The cycle of seasons by which many churches walk through the life of Christ each year, from Advent to Pentecost. Some churches keep it; others keep only the Lord's Day.
Latin for remember that you must die: the practice, long kept by Christians, of keeping one's death in view so that it shapes how one lives.
One of the passages in the second half of Isaiah about the servant of the LORD; the best known, Isaiah 52:13-53:12, the church has read from its first days as a portrait of Jesus.
The week before Easter, from Palm Sunday to Holy Saturday, remembering Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, the Last Supper, his death, and his rest in the tomb.
The Thursday of Holy Week, remembering the Last Supper. Its name comes from the Latin word for commandment, after Jesus' new commandment to love one another (John 13:34).
From the Latin word for suffering. The passion of Christ is his suffering and death, which Mark tells in chapters 14 and 15.
The day Jesus' body lay in the tomb, which the women kept as a Sabbath (Luke 23:56). Many churches keep it quietly, some with a vigil that night.
The feast of the resurrection of Jesus, called Pascha in many churches, from the word for Passover. Every Sunday also celebrates it.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Lent is often kept in one of two wrong ways, as a diet with a religious label or as forty days of feeling bad, and many churches don't keep it at all. This five-session study walks from Ash Wednesday to the sealed tomb of Holy Saturday: dust and mercy, Jesus' forty days in the wilderness, Joel's call to return and David's prayer in Psalm 51, the way of the cross in Mark 8 and Isaiah 53, and the darkest week in Mark 14 and 15. It is for those who have kept Lent all their lives and those who never have. Fasting is voluntary and comes with health cautions first, and a volunteer can lead each session after reading the leader's primer once.

You don't have to fast, you don't have to receive ashes, and no one will ask what you gave up. It's five sessions through passages many churches read in this season: dust and mercy, the wilderness, returning to God, the way of the cross, and the last week of Jesus' life in Mark. It's for people who have kept Lent all their lives and for anyone who wonders why anyone would. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: "For dust you are, and to dust you shall return" (Genesis 3:19). A five-session study for Lent, from Ash Wednesday to the sealed tomb, for those who have kept it all their lives and those who never have. No one has to fast. Come and walk the forty days.
quoteCards: Ash Wednesday tells the truth about us in public, to everyone at once. We are dust, and we are remembered.
In Psalm 103 our frailty is the reason for God's gentleness. He knows our frame.
Temptation rarely offers something monstrous. It offers something good by the wrong road.
A fast is hunger turned toward God, kept quietly, and it ends at a table.
Repentance is turning around and coming home to a God who was gracious before we turned.
Before the cross is the shape of our following, it is what Christ carried for us.
Taking up the cross never means staying where you are being hurt.
The women stayed when the men had fled, and they saw where he was laid. Saturday belongs to the Christian story too.
